Frequency table for one column

Source: R/dsc.R
freqtbl.Rd

Counts how often each value of a column occurs, with percentages of all rows and of the non-missing rows, and missing values counted as their own row. It is the first look at a categorical variable (a charge type, a region, a response category).

Usage

freqtbl(data, col = NULL, maxlvl = 25L, sort = TRUE)

# S3 method for class 'freqtbl'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame, or a vector.

col

Column name (a string), when data is a data frame; ignored for a vector.

maxlvl

Maximum value rows to return, most frequent first (default 25). The remainder are folded into one "(other)" row so the percentages still sum to 100.

sort

Logical: sort by descending count (default TRUE); FALSE keeps the sorted order of the values.

x

A result of freqtbl().

...

Not used.

Value

A data frame of class c("freqtbl", "data.frame") with columns value (character), n (integer count), pct (numeric, percent of all rows) and pctvalid (numeric, percent of non-missing rows; NA on the missing row).

Details

Two percentage columns, because both questions get asked and conflating them is how missingness gets hidden: pct is the share of ALL rows, pctvalid the share of rows where the value is present. When a column is 40\ the values that are actually there.

Values are tabulated as text (as.character()), so numbers and factors are counted by their printed value, and factor levels that do not occur get no row. Rows are sorted by descending count (ties in the order table() gives) or kept in sorted value order with sort = FALSE. Beyond maxlvl distinct values, the rest are folded into one "(other)" row so the percentages still sum to 100. The missing row, when there is one, comes last, with value NA and pctvalid NA. An empty input gives a table with no rows. The print method adds a bar column.

Errors: a data frame without col; a col that is not in data; maxlvl not one positive whole number.

See also

profcols for every column at once.

Examples

df <- data.frame(grade = c("a", "b", "b", "c", NA, "b"))
freqtbl(df, "grade")
#> Frequency table: 6 values
#>  value n      pct pctvalid                  bar
#>      b 3 50.00000       60 ####################
#>      a 1 16.66667       20              #######
#>      c 1 16.66667       20              #######
#>   <NA> 1 16.66667       NA              #######

# The two percentage columns differ exactly by the missingness.
freqtbl(df, "grade")[, c("pct", "pctvalid")]
#>       pct pctvalid
#>  50.00000       60
#>  16.66667       20
#>  16.66667       20
#>  16.66667       NA

# A vector works directly.
freqtbl(c(1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3))
#> Frequency table: 6 values
#>  value n      pct pctvalid                  bar
#>      3 3 50.00000 50.00000 ####################
#>      1 2 33.33333 33.33333        #############
#>      2 1 16.66667 16.66667              #######

# Sorted value order rather than frequency order.
freqtbl(c("c", "a", "b", "a"), sort = FALSE)
#> Frequency table: 4 values
#>  value n pct pctvalid                  bar
#>      a 2  50       50 ####################
#>      b 1  25       25           ##########
#>      c 1  25       25           ##########

# Long tails are folded so the percentages still total 100.
set.seed(1)
ft <- freqtbl(sample(letters, 500, TRUE), maxlvl = 5)
ft
#> Frequency table: 500 values
#>    value   n  pct pctvalid                  bar
#>        y  25  5.0      5.0                    #
#>        e  24  4.8      4.8                    #
#>        t  24  4.8      4.8                    #
#>        a  23  4.6      4.6                    #
#>        f  23  4.6      4.6                    #
#>  (other) 381 76.2     76.2 ####################
sum(ft$pct)
#> [1] 100

# a data frame needs a column name
try(freqtbl(df))
#> Error : freqtbl: `col` is required when `data` is a data frame.
